hints: Focus on the strict definition of standard enthalpy of formation, forming exactly 1 mol of product only from its elements.
Check each equation for two things, is only 1 mol of product made, and are all reactants elements in their standard states under standard conditions?
Remember carbon is a solid as graphite and chlorine and oxygen are diatomic gases, so spot which equation breaks the elements-only rule.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of formation**

Enthalpy of formation is special. It is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements, with all substances in their standard states.

$$\text{elements in standard states} \rightarrow 1 \text{ mol of compound}$$

**List the three checks to pass**

First, there must be exactly 1 mol of one product. Second, all reactants must be elements, not compounds. Third, each element must be in its standard state.

Standard states to remember: $\text{C(s)}$ as graphite, $\text{H}_2(g)$, $\text{N}_2(g)$, $\text{O}_2(g)$, $\text{Cl}_2(g)$.

**Test each reaction**

Option B fits perfectly. $\frac{1}{2}\text{N}_2(g) + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{NO}(g)$ makes 1 mol of $\text{NO}$ from only elements in standard states. The fractions are allowed to get 1 mol of product.

The others fail one check, so only one reaction is a true formation reaction.

options.A: Incorrect. Although it makes 1 mol of $\text{CH}_4(g)$ from elements only, carbon is not in its standard state. Standard carbon is solid graphite, $\text{C(s)}$, not $\text{C(g)}$. This is a common trap.
options.B: Correct. Exactly 1 mol of $\text{NO}(g)$ is formed from its elements $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$, both in their standard states as gases. The $\frac{1}{2}$ coefficients are correct and needed to make 1 mol of product.
options.C: Incorrect. Although it makes 1 mol of $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(s)$, the reactants $\text{Na}_2\text{O}(s)$ and $\text{SO}_3(g)$ are compounds, not elements. Formation must start only from elements.
options.D: Incorrect. Although it makes 1 mol of $\text{PCl}_5(g)$, the reactant $\text{PCl}_3(g)$ is a compound, not an element. Only $\text{Cl}_2(g)$ is an element here.
